chunks.text: Summary: This practice guidance reviews the epidemiology, physiology, risk factors, and types of hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated and gadolinium-based contrast media. It evaluates evidence for premedication protocols and allergy investigations, and provides consensus recommendations to inform hospital policies and reduce breakthrough reactions.

chunks.text:
Conditions:
  Condition id: cond_01
  Name: Hypersensitivity Reaction to Contrast Media
  Synonyms:
    - contrast media allergy
    - allergic-like reaction
    - contrast media hypersensitivity
  Description: Adverse immune-mediated responses to iodinated contrast media or gadolinium-based contrast agents following intravenous injection, presenting along a spectrum from mild urticaria to life-threatening anaphylaxis. These reactions are triggered by the contrast molecule itself, not by iodine.
  Epidemiology: Immediate hypersensitivity reactions to low osmolar contrast media arise in approximately 0.38% of administrations, with severe events in 0.02%; delayed reactions occur in 0.05%. For gadolinium-based contrast agents, hypersensitivity reactions are documented in less than 0.4% of uses, and anaphylaxis rates range from 0.00003% to 0.004%. Key risk factors include a prior hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media, atopic history, female sex, and higher contrast concentration or injection rate.
  Clinical presentation: Immediate reactions (within 1 hour) manifest as urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. Delayed reactions (hours to days later) usually present as maculopapular exanthema, with rare severe cutaneous adverse events such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, or Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.
  Subtypes:
    - Name: Immediate Hypersensitivity Reaction
      Distinguishing features: Develops within 1 hour of contrast administration; can be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated; may progress to anaphylaxis with cardiovascular compromise.
    - Name: Delayed Hypersensitivity Reaction
      Distinguishing features: Appears hours to days after exposure; predominantly T-cell driven; usually mild skin eruptions but occasionally severe systemic reactions.
  Diagnostic workup:
    - Test: Allergy skin testing
      Purpose: Identify the responsible contrast agent and assess cross-reactivity among agents
      When indicated: After a severe hypersensitivity reaction to guide selection of a safe alternative contrast medium
      Interpretation: Cross-reactivity on skin testing correlates with shared side chains between iodinated contrast media; choosing an agent with a different side chain lowers the risk of recurrence.
  Staging:
    System: American College of Radiology severity classification (mild, moderate, severe)
    Additional rules: Detailed definitions appear in Appendix A of the source guideline (not included in the present extraction).

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_01
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with a history of mild immediate hypersensitivity reaction to iodinated contrast media (e.g., limited urticaria, pruritus)
  Decision rules:
    - If the prior reaction was mild (isolated urticaria), consider no premedication or premedication with a second-generation antihistamine.
    - Contrast switching may further reduce risk but is not always necessary.
    - Avoid first-generation antihistamines due to side effects.
    - Corticosteroid premedication is not recommended due to lack of strong evidence and potential harms.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication
      Summary: Administer a second-generation oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 10 mg) 1-2 hours prior to contrast administration. This may reduce breakthrough reactions from 16.6% to 10.7% (OR 0.569, 95% CI 0.443-0.731).
      Key outcomes: Reduction in mild breakthrough reaction rate
      Duration cycles: Single dose before procedure
    - Name: No premedication (optional)
      Summary: In patients with isolated urticaria, some centers have abandoned premedication as there is no proven benefit with antihistamines.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Switch to a different low-osmolar ICM with a different side chain
      Summary: Switching the ICM agent reduces the risk of breakthrough reactions by 61% (risk ratio 0.39, 95% credible interval 0.24-0.58) and is an effective strategy, especially if premedication fails.
      Conditions for use: When repeat reaction occurs despite premedication or if patient preference.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Corticosteroid premedication
      Reason: Evidence does not support efficacy; NNT to prevent one reaction of any severity is 69 (95% CI 39-304), and for severe reactions 569 (95% CI 389-1083). Potential harms include delayed hospital stay, fractures, infections.
    - Name: First-generation antihistamines
      Reason: Lower safety and efficacy profile; CSACI recommends second/third generation antihistamines.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: During and up to 1 hour after contrast administration
      Method: Clinical monitoring for signs of hypersensitivity (urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension)
      Interpretation: If breakthrough reaction occurs, treat per anaphylaxis guidelines.
  Supportive care:
    - Ensure availability of emergency anaphylaxis medications (epinephrine, antihistamines, IV fluids).
    - Patient education on recognizing and reporting symptoms.
  Special considerations: For mild reactions, antihistamine alone may suffice. Documentation of specific culprit agent is critical for future management.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_02
  Condition ref: cond_01
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with a history of moderate to severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to ICM (e.g., diffuse urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis)
  Decision rules:
    - Contrast switching is the most effective strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions.
    - Select an ICM with a different side chain structure (see Table 1) to minimize cross-reactivity.
    - Premedication with antihistamines may be added but evidence is limited.
    - Corticosteroid premedication is not routinely recommended due to lack of strong efficacy and potential harms.
    - Consider allergy consultation and skin testing (skin prick, intradermal) 2-6 months after the reaction to guide choice.
    - If urgent imaging required and no time for testing, switch to a structurally different ICM and consider accelerated IV corticosteroid protocol (5-hour) as an alternative, though efficacy is uncertain.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Switch to a different low-osmolar ICM
      Summary: Switching to an ICM with a different chemical structure reduces the risk of recurrent immediate hypersensitivity; breakthrough reaction rates dropped from 27.7% (same ICM without premedication) to 2.9% (different ICM without premedication). Substitution with a structurally different agent had OR 0.51 (95% CI 0.37-0.69) for repeat reaction.
      Key outcomes: Reduction in breakthrough reaction rate to approximately 3-8%
    - Name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (optional)
      Summary: May be added but evidence is limited; in one study, switching plus premedication did not show significant difference from switching alone.
      Duration cycles: Single dose prior to contrast
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Accelerated IV corticosteroid premedication (5-hour protocol) with antihistamine
      Summary: An accelerated 5-hour IV corticosteroid protocol was non-inferior to traditional 13-hour oral regimen in preventing breakthrough reactions (2.5% vs 2.1%), but neither prevented all moderate/severe reactions. May be considered when prolonged oral protocol is not feasible and rapid imaging needed.
      Conditions for use: When urgent imaging is required and oral premedication cannot be completed.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Routine corticosteroid premedication (oral or IV) as sole strategy
      Reason: Insufficient evidence for efficacy; potential harms outweigh benefits. NNT to prevent severe reaction is 569 (95% CI 389-1083).
    - Name: Re-using the same ICM agent without switching
      Reason: Higher breakthrough reaction rates (19% with premedication, 15% without).
    - Name: First-generation antihistamines
      Reason: Higher side effect profile; not recommended by CSACI.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: During and for at least 30-60 minutes after contrast administration
      Method: Continuous monitoring for signs of anaphylaxis; consider serum tryptase measurement if reaction occurs
      Interpretation: Treat any breakthrough reaction immediately per anaphylaxis protocol.
  Supportive care:
    - Ensure immediate availability of emergency drugs and equipment (epinephrine auto-injector, IV access, oxygen).
    - Document the specific contrast agent and reaction details in the medical record and imaging report.
  Special considerations: Allergy consultation is recommended for severe reactions (anaphylaxis) before re-exposure. Skin testing may identify safe alternatives.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_03
  Condition ref: cond_02
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with a history of immediate hypersensitivity reaction to gadolinium-based contrast agents (any severity)
  Decision rules:
    - Contrast switching is the most effective strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions.
    - Switch to a GBCA of a different class (e.g., from linear ionic to macrocyclic) and different molecular structure.
    - Premedication with antihistamines or corticosteroids is of uncertain benefit.
    - The incidence of HRs to GBCAs is very low overall.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Switch to a different GBCA (different class/molecular structure)
      Summary: Switching the GBCA reduced breakthrough reaction rates significantly: from 25.8% (same GBCA) to 6.9% (different GBCA) in one study. In another, switching with or without premedication resulted in a 3.7% breakthrough rate. Switching alone had OR 0.3 (95% CI 0.2-0.5).
      Key outcomes: Breakthrough reaction rate approximately 3.7-6.9% with switching
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (if switching not possible or added precaution)
      Summary: May be considered, but evidence shows no significant difference between premedicated and non-premedicated groups when switching is done.
      Conditions for use: When only one GBCA is available or patient refuses switching.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Corticosteroid premedication without switching
      Reason: No clear benefit; switching alone appears sufficient and avoids steroid risks.
    - Name: Re-using the same GBCA
      Reason: Higher breakthrough reaction rates (19.0% with premedication, 31.4% without).
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: During and for 30 minutes after GBCA injection
      Method: Clinical monitoring for hypersensitivity signs
      Interpretation: Manage any breakthrough reaction as per anaphylaxis guidelines.
  Supportive care:
    - Anaphylaxis emergency kit available.
    - Document the culprit GBCA and reaction details in the health record.
  Special considerations: For severe reactions, consider allergy evaluation. Skin testing is less sensitive for GBCA; provocation challenges may be considered under specialist supervision.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_04
  Condition ref: cond_03
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with a history of delayed hypersensitivity reactions to contrast media (ICM or GBCA), such as maculopapular exanthem
  Decision rules:
    - Premedication is not recommended for prevention of delayed HRs.
    - Contrast switching is the preferred strategy if re-exposure is necessary.
    - Allergy investigations (patch testing, delayed intradermal testing) can be considered to identify safe alternatives, but are not mandatory.
    - Corticosteroid premedication does not reliably prevent delayed reactions.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Switch to a different contrast agent (structurally different class)
      Summary: Use an alternate ICM or GBCA with a different chemical structure. Avoid the culprit agent. Premedication is not recommended.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Premedication with corticosteroids or antihistamines
      Reason: No evidence of efficacy for delayed reactions; may cause unnecessary side effects.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Hours to days after exposure
      Method: Patient education to report delayed skin eruptions; consider follow-up if needed
  Special considerations: Document the onset and nature of the index reaction to avoid premedication confusion. In severe delayed reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS), avoid all contrast media if possible.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_05
  Condition ref: cond_04
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Patients with prior hypersensitivity reaction to intravascular contrast media who require non-vascular contrast (enteric, etc.)
  Decision rules:
    - The working group does not endorse premedication for non-vascular contrast media administration.
    - Adverse reactions to non-vascular contrast are very rare.
    - If the patient has a history of reaction to non-vascular contrast itself, consider switching the agent.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: No premedication
      Summary: Administer non-vascular contrast without premedication. Risk of reaction is extremely low.
  Alternative regimens:
    - Name: Switch non-vascular contrast agent if prior reaction to that specific agent
      Summary: Consider using a different non-vascular contrast medium (e.g., different iodine concentration or brand) if there is a documented reaction to the previous non-vascular agent.
      Conditions for use: Only if there is a known reaction to non-vascular contrast.
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Premedication for non-vascular procedures
      Reason: No evidence to support its use; reactions are rare.
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: Routine observation
      Method: Standard post-procedure monitoring if any systemic absorption is expected
  Special considerations: If the non-vascular contrast could be absorbed or leak into the circulation (e.g., during procedures), follow same precautions as intravascular administration.

chunks.text:
Treatment pathways:
  Pathway id: path_06
  Condition ref: cond_05
  Setting: first_line
  Patient population: Pediatric patients (children) with a history of hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media (ICM or GBCA)
  Decision rules:
    - Pediatric patients have lower baseline HR rates than adults (adjusted OR 0.58 for ICM).
    - Management is similar to adults, with weight-adjusted doses.
    - Premedication with corticosteroids should be avoided in children due to risk of infections, behavioral changes, and fractures.
    - Contrast switching is preferred.
  Recommended regimens:
    - Name: Switch to a different contrast agent (weight-appropriate dose)
      Summary: Use an alternative ICM or GBCA as per adult guidelines. Dose based on weight.
    - Name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (if deemed necessary)
      Summary: If premedication is considered, use a second-generation antihistamine at pediatric weight-based dosing.
      Duration cycles: Single dose before procedure
  Not recommended:
    - Name: Corticosteroid premedication in children
      Reason: Short-course oral corticosteroids in children are associated with vomiting, behavioral changes, sleep disturbance, and infections; risk of fracture (OR 1.17).
  Response assessment:
    - Timepoint: During and after contrast administration
      Method: Monitoring appropriate for pediatric patients; have pediatric emergency equipment
      Interpretation: Manage any reaction per pediatric anaphylaxis guidelines.
  Supportive care:
    - Ensure pediatric resuscitation equipment available.
  Special considerations: Fasting prior to contrast is not recommended in children unless specifically required for the procedure.

chunks.text:
Therapies index:
  Name: Diphenhydramine
  Type: drug
  Mechanism: First-generation H1 receptor antagonist
  Approved indications:
    - Prevention of hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated contrast media
  Administration: Oral 25–50 mg or intramuscular 50 mg
  Key toxicities:
    - Sedation
    - Anticholinergic effects
    - Cardiac toxicity
    - Respiratory depression
    - Impaired sleep quality

chunks.text:
Therapies index:
  Name: Greenberger Premedication Protocol
  Type: regimen
  Components:
    - Prednisone
    - Diphenhydramine
  Mechanism: Prophylactic premedication combining a corticosteroid and an antihistamine to reduce allergic-like reactions to contrast media
  Approved indications:
    - Prevention of hypersensitivity reactions in patients with prior reaction to high-osmolality contrast media (historical), now used for low-osmolality contrast media
  Administration: Oral prednisone 50 mg every 6 hours for three doses, with intramuscular diphenhydramine 50 mg 1 hour before contrast procedure
  Key toxicities:
    - Sedation
    - Anticholinergic effects
    - Corticosteroid-related adverse events (fracture, sepsis, VTE)

Therapies index:
  Name: Contrast Media Switching
  Type: procedure
  Mechanism: Substitution of the iodinated contrast agent with one having a different side chain structure to minimize cross-reactivity and breakth
  Approved indications:
    - Prevention of recurrent hypersensitivity reactions in patients with a history of immediate hypersensitivity to iodinated contrast media
  Administration: Selection of an alternative low-osmolar contrast medium that does not share the N-(2,3-dihydroxypropyl)-N-methyl-carbamoyl or N-(2,3-dihydroxypropyl) carbamoyl side chain with the culprit agent
  Monitoring:
    - Document exact name of prior culprit agent
    - Monitor for breakthrough reactions

chunks.text:
Toxicities:
  Event: Hypersensitivity reactions to contrast media
  Associated therapies:
    - iodinated contrast media
    - gadolinium-based contrast agents
  Incidence: Acute HR rates: LOCM ~0.4%–3.13%, GBCA ~0.4% (overall), macrocyclic GBCA 14/10,000, linear ionic 8.3/10,000, linear nonionic 1.5/10,000. Breakthrough rates: same ICM without premedication 15%, with premedication 19%, different ICM 3% (McDonald 2021); same GBCA without premedication 31.4%, with premedication 19.0%, different GBCA without premedication 6.0%, with premedication 4.8% (Ahn 2022).
  Recognition:
    - Urticaria, pruritus, cutaneous edema, nasal congestion, sneezing, conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea
    - Throat tightness, hoarseness, wheezing, bronchospasm, hypoxia
    - Facial edema, diffuse erythema, hypotension
    - Anaphylactic shock (hypotension, tachycardia)
    - Delayed reactions: maculopapular exanthem, SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP
  Grading: ACR categories: Mild (self-limited, no treatment needed), Moderate (require medical management, some may progress), Severe (life-threatening, may cause permanent morbidity or death)
  Prevention:
    - Contrast agent switching is effective in reducing recurrent reactions.
    - Routine premedication with corticosteroids and/or antihistamines is not recommended; evidence is weak and potential harms exist.
    - For severe index reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS), consider allergy consultation and skin/intradermal testing for alternative agents.

chunks.text:
Toxicities:
  Event: Adverse effects of premedication (corticosteroids and antihistamines)
  Associated therapies:
    - corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, methylprednisolone)
    - first-generation antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine)
  Incidence: Projected harms per prevented contrast-related death: 551 hospital-acquired infections, 32 infection-related deaths. NNT to prevent one lethal reaction: 56,900 (95% CI 38,900–108,300). Short-term oral corticosteroid risks: avascular necrosis RR 1.60 (95% CI 1.34–1.84), bone fracture in children OR 1.17 (95% CI 1.04–1.33). Pediatric corticosteroid course (<14 days) may cause vomiting, behavioral changes, mood swings, sleep disturbance, and infections.
  Recognition:
    - First-generation antihistamines: sedation, poor sleep quality, cardiac toxicity, respiratory depression, coma, death.
    - Corticosteroids: hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood disturbances, avascular necrosis, infections, fractures, venous thromboembolism.
  Prevention:
    - CSACI recommends using second/third-generation antihistamines over first-generation agents.
    - Avoid routine corticosteroid premedication; balance potential benefits against risks.
    - Consider an accelerated 5-hour IV corticosteroid regimen if urgent premedication is deemed necessary (non-inferior to 13-hour oral protocol but does not eliminate all moderate/severe reactions).

Prophylaxis:
  - Type: contrast_media_hypersensitivity
    Recommendation: Routine premedication with corticosteroids and/or antihistamines is not recommended due to insufficient evidence and potential harms. Switching to a structurally different contrast agent is the preferred strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions. For patients with severe prior reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS), allergy consultation and skin testing may guide selection of an alternative agent.

chunks.text:
Recommendations:
  - Rec id: rec_01
    Statement: The exact dose and specific name of any contrast medium must be recorded in the patient's electronic health record for easy retrieval in case of a hypersensitivity reaction. Following an acute reaction, the culprit agent's name must be documented in the radiology report, which is sent to the referring clinician and archived in PACS. Additionally, the timing, characteristics, and management of the reaction should be documented. A system for reporting delayed hypersensitivity reactions should be established.
    Rationale: Proper documentation ensures that the offending agent can be identified and avoided in future examinations, facilitating contrast switching.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_02
    Statement: The sole risk factor for a future hypersensitivity reaction is a prior hypersensitivity reaction to the identical type of contrast medium (i.e., LOCM ICM or GBCA). No other risk factors warrant routine screening. Clinicians must differentiate between true hypersensitivity and physiologic reactions.
    Rationale: Evidence indicates that only previous HR to the same contrast type consistently predicts future reactions; screening other purported risk factors is not evidence-based.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_03
    Statement: In patients with any severity of prior hypersensitivity reaction to ICM or GBCA, administering a chemically distinct contrast agent is the most effective strategy to prevent a recurrent reaction. If a mild or moderate breakthrough reaction occurs despite switching, a third agent should be used. Institutions must maintain at least two different contrast agents; sole-supplier contracts should permit procurement of an alternative agent.
    Rationale: Studies show that contrast switching significantly reduces breakthrough reaction rates compared to re-challenge with the same agent.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_04
    Statement: When the culprit ICM is unknown, management depends on the timing and severity of the antecedent reaction. If the reaction occurred before 2000, the agent was likely not low-osmolality, and current LOCM can be administered without premedication. For reactions on or after 2000: if severe, consider an alternative imaging modality or allergy consultation; premedication is not advised. If mild or moderate, premedication with second-generation antihistamines and close monitoring is suggested.
    Rationale: Prior to 2000, high-osmolality contrast media were commonly used; reactions to those agents are not predictive of reactions to modern low-osmolality agents.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_05
    Statement: Steroid premedication for patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to LOCM is not justified by high-quality evidence; existing studies are methodologically weak and involved HOCM. Given the lack of efficacy and potential harms, the routine use of corticosteroids for prophylaxis in high-risk patients is discouraged and should be abandoned.
    Rationale: No robust evidence supports corticosteroid premedication for LOCM; historic data on HOCM are not applicable, and steroids carry risks of adverse effects and increased hospitalization.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_06
    Statement: For patients with a previous hypersensitivity reaction to GBCA, corticosteroid premedication is not advised. The evidence is conflicting, but the net benefit is minimal and potential harms exist.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_07
    Statement: Second-generation antihistamines may reduce breakthrough reactions in patients with a history of mild hypersensitivity. Their additional benefit after contrast switching is uncertain and may be considered optional. Oral second-generation antihistamines should be administered at least 1 hour before contrast injection.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_08
    Statement: There is currently inadequate evidence to prefer any specific LOCM product for reducing hypersensitivity reactions. Although preliminary data suggest that the choice of agent for contrast switching might be based on molecular structure, this evidence is insufficient to warrant a formal recommendation.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_09
    Statement: Differences in hypersensitivity rates among GBCAs exist but are small, and the absolute risk of a reaction is extremely low. Therefore, the selection of a specific GBCA should be guided by factors such as cost, diagnostic need, and T1 relaxivity.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_10
    Statement: In patients with prior contrast-induced anaphylaxis, using an alternative imaging method that does not require contrast is preferred to minimize breakthrough reaction risk. If contrast is necessary, switch to a different agent and monitor the patient closely during and after administration. Premedication should not be used.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_11
    Statement: After stabilization of a patient with anaphylaxis, obtain serum tryptase 30–120 minutes after symptom onset to aid in confirming an immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Referral to an allergist should be considered if feasible.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_12
    Statement: In patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to nonvascular contrast agents, future administration—whether vascular or nonvascular—should involve switching to a different agent without premedication. Adverse events after nonvascular contrast are extremely rare and not well documented; thus, premedication is not supported.
    Source heading: Recommendations
  - Rec id: rec_13
    Statement: Patients should not be required to fast before intravascular contrast administration, unless the examination itself demands it (e.g., CT or MR enterography).
    Source heading: Recommendations

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_03
  Type: table
  Title: A Summary of Guidelines From Other Societies Specific to Iodinated Contrast Media
  Source heading: Overview of Existing Guidelines
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Society guideline: European Society of Urogenital Radiology (2019)
      Prevention - acute hr: Use an alternate contrast agent; base this choice on investigations. Prophylaxis is not recommended.
      Prevention - delayed hr: Consider patch testing. Use a different contrast agent. Prophylaxis not recommended.
      Investigations - acute hr: Consider serum histamine and tryptase collection during and after the reaction. SPT/ID testing 1-6mo after the event.
      Investigations - delayed hr: Consider ID testing with delayed interpretation. Any patient with a maculopapular exanthem should be investigated.
    Row 2:
      Society guideline: European Academy of Allergy and Clinical Immunology (2020)
      Prevention - acute hr: Use an alternate contrast agent, as guided by investigations. Prophylaxis is not recommended.
      Prevention - delayed hr: Prophylaxis is not recommended (can be considered if previous contrast trigger not identified, or if testing not complete in an emergency).
      Investigations - acute hr: Consider serum tryptase during and after the reaction. SPT/ID testing 2-6mo after the event. Consider use of BAT. Consider drug provocation if favourable risk/benefit ratio.
      Investigations - delayed hr: Tests to consider include patch testing, ID testing, or LTT.
    Row 3:
      Society guideline: American Academy of Asthma, Allergy, and Immunology: Anaphylaxis practice parameter update (2020)
      Prevention - acute hr: No recommendations made
      Prevention - delayed hr: Prophylaxis is generally not recommended (for LOCM contrast), though there may be conditional exceptions, including high level of perceived risk of anaphylaxis fatality, though evidence is lacking to support this approach.
      Investigations - acute hr: No investigations are recommended.
      Investigations - delayed hr: No investigations are recommended.
    Row 4:
      Society guideline: American College of Radiology (2023)
      Prevention - acute hr: Prophylaxis may be of some benefit, though there is no specific recommendation. Consider alternate contrast agent.
      Prevention - delayed hr: Prophylaxis (steroids, antihistamines) is recommended combined with changing the class of agent.
      Investigations - acute hr: No investigations are recommended.
      Investigations - delayed hr: No investigations are recommended. The effectiveness of premedication with corticosteroids in reducing the incidence of recurrent delayed contrast media reaction is unknown.
    Row 5:
      Society guideline: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Radiologists (2018) / Endorsed by the Royal College of Radiologists (UK)
      Prevention - acute hr: Premedication with corticosteroids, with or without antihistamines has been shown to reduce the likelihood and severity of anaphylactic reactions but there is no evidence that it reduces the likelihood of death resulting from a breakthrough anaphylactic reaction.
    Row 6:
      Society guideline: Korean Academy of Asthma, Allergy and Clinical Immunology (2022)
      Prevention - acute hr: If severe, avoid contrast if possible. If impossible, base alternate choice on allergy testing if favourable risk-benefit ratio.
      Prevention - delayed hr: Avoid use of contrast if possible. If contrast to be used, use alternate agent with prophylaxis, if testing previously unavailable.
      Investigations - acute hr: SP/ID testing with trigger ICM and alternates. Consider IV DPT challenge to alternate media if needed.
      Investigations - delayed hr: All patients with non-severe reactions should use alternate ICM if urgent, or complete testing if time allows. If previously investigated, use alternate contrast choice. Prophylaxis, in general, not recommended, but may be considered if high risk individuals with severe HR's.
  Summary: Comparison of recommendations from various international guidelines regarding prevention and investigation of acute and delayed hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated contrast media.
  Clinical relevance: Highlights the lack of consensus and evolving evidence, guiding clinicians to adopt practices such as contrast switching over standard premedication protocols.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_04
  Type: flowchart
  Title: Figure 1: Hypersensitivity reaction to LOCM or GBCA
  Source heading: Conclusions
  Description: Step 1: Patient has a history of hypersensitivity reaction to a specific low-osmolality contrast medium (LOCM) or gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCA). Step 2: Switch to a chemically different contrast agent. Step 3: If no breakthrough reaction occurs, proceed with routine monitoring. Step 4: If a mild or moderate breakthrough reaction occurs after switching, administer a third, different contrast agent. Step 5: If a severe breakthrough reaction occurs, consider an alternative imaging modality or allergy consultation.
  Summary: Algorithm for managing patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to a known contrast agent, emphasizing contrast switching as the primary preventive measure.
  Clinical relevance: Provides a structured approach to minimize risk of recurrent reactions, reducing reliance on premedication and guiding appropriate use of alternative agents.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_05
  Type: flowchart
  Title: Figure 2: Hypersensitivity reaction to ICM unknown agent
  Source heading: Conclusions
  Description: Step 1: Patient has a history of hypersensitivity reaction to iodinated contrast media (ICM) but the offending agent is unknown. Step 2: Determine if the reaction occurred before or after the year 2000. Step 3a: If before 2000, the agent was likely not a low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM); administer LOCM without premedication. Step 3b: If on or after 2000 and the reaction was severe (acute or delayed), consider an alternative imaging modality; if contrast is essential, consider allergy referral; premedication is not recommended. Step 3c: If on or after 2000 and the reaction was mild or moderate, consider premedication with second-generation antihistamines and monitor closely.
  Summary: Decision tree for patients with an uncertain history of ICM hypersensitivity, using the date and severity of the index reaction to guide management.
  Clinical relevance: Helps clinicians safely manage patients when the culprit contrast agent cannot be identified, balancing the need for contrast-enhanced imaging with the risk of recurrence.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_06
  Type: table
  Title: Appendix A: American College of Radiology Categories of Acute Reactions
  Source heading: Appendix A
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Severity: Mild
      Allergic-like (hypersensitivity):
        - Limited urticaria/pruritis
        - Cutaneous oedema
        - Limited "itchy"/"scratchy" throat
        - Nasal congestion
        - Sneezing/conjunctivitis/rhinorrhoea
      Physiologic:
        - Limited nausea/vomiting limited
        - Transient flushing/warmth/chills
        - Headache/dizziness/anxiety/altered taste
        - Mild hypertension
        - Vasovagal reaction that resolves spontaneously
    Row 2:
      Severity: Moderate
      Allergic-like (hypersensitivity):
        - Diffuse urticaria/pruritis
        - Diffuse erythema, stable vital signs
        - Facial oedema without dyspnoea
        - Throat tightness or hoarseness without dyspnoea
        - Wheezing/bronchospasm, mild or no hypoxia
      Physiologic:
        - Protracted nausea/vomiting
        - Hypertensive urgency
        - Isolated chest pain
        - Vasovagal reaction that requires and is responsive to treatment
    Row 3:
      Severity: Severe
      Allergic-like (hypersensitivity):
        - Diffuse oedema, or facial oedema with dyspnoea
        - Diffuse erythema with hypotension
        - Laryngeal oedema with stridor and/or hypoxia
        - Wheezing/bronchospasm, significant hypoxia
        - Anaphylactic shock (hypotension+ tachycardia)
      Physiologic:
        - Vasovagal reaction resistant to treatment
        - Arrhythmia
        - Convulsions, seizures
        - Hypertensive emergency
  Summary: Classification of acute contrast reactions by severity, distinguishing between allergic-like and physiologic manifestations.
  Clinical relevance: Standardizes assessment and management of contrast reactions, ensuring timely and appropriate interventions based on symptom severity.

chunks.text:
Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_08
  Type: table
  Title: Appendix C: Commercially Available Biomarkers of Anaphylaxis
  Source heading: Appendix C
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Biomarker: Serum tryptase
      Normal values: ≤11.4ng/mL
      Test protocol: Draw 1-6h after exposure to allergen, best 1-2h after symptom onset.
      Pros:
        - High specificity
        - No sample storage requirements
      Cons: Negative in up to 40% of cases of anaphylaxis
      Citation: Schwartz et al107 Sala-Cunill et al108
    Row 2:
      Biomarker: Serum Histamine
      Normal values: <10nmol/L
      Test protocol: Levels peak 5-15min after allergen exposure, returns to normal 10-30min later.
      Pros: High specificity
      Cons:
        - Sample requires freezing. Falsely elevated in histamine rich foods
        - Short half-life 2min
      Citation: Oosting et al109 Hogan and Scwartz110 van Doormaal et al111 Tomasiak-Łozowska et al112
    Row 3:
      Biomarker: Urine N-methylhistamine
      Normal values: 176µmol/mol cr
      Test protocol: Detectable within 30-60min of anaphylaxis.
      Pros: High specificity Sensitivity 0.81, specificity 0.93.
      Cons:
        - Falsely elevated in histamine rich foods.
        - Normal values extrapolated from systemic mastocytosis patients.
        - Requires 24h urine collection.
      Citation: Lin et al113
  Summary: Lists biomarkers for confirming mast cell activation during anaphylaxis, with practical considerations for collection timing and diagnostic accuracy.
  Clinical relevance: Serum tryptase is the most practical biomarker in Canada; measuring it 30-120 minutes after symptom onset aids in retrospectively confirming an immediate hypersensitivity reaction.

Artifacts:
  Artifact id: art_09
  Type: table
  Title: Appendix D: Diagnostic Tests in Contrast Media Hypersensitivity
  Source heading: Appendix D
  Data:
    Row 1:
      Test: Skin Prick Test—Immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 3% positive
      Test protocol: Read at 20min; undiluted contrast media
      Citation: Yoon et al97 Brockow et al15
    Row 2:
      Test: Skin Prick Test—Non-immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 7% positive
      Test protocol: Read at day 2-3; undiluted contrast media
      Citation: Yoon et al97 Brockow et al15
    Row 3:
      Test: Intradermal Test—immediate HR
      Test outcomes: Positive rate higher when performed 1-6mo following reaction. Mild reactions—12% positive; Moderate reactions—16% positive; Severe reactions—52% positive
      Test protocol: Read at 20min; 1:10 dilution contrast media
      Citation: Yoon et al97 Brockow et al15
    Row 4:
      Test: Intradermal Test—non immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 22% positive
      Test protocol: Read at days 1, 2, 3; 1:10 dilution contrast media
      Citation: Yoon et al97 Brockow et al15
    Row 5:
      Test: Patch test—Non immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 16% positive
      Test protocol: Read at 48 and 72h; undiluted, soaked in filter paper
      Citation: Pinnobphun et al114
    Row 6:
      Test: Basophil Activation Test—Immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 1:10 dilution has 61.5% sensitivity, 76.7% specificity; 1:100 dilution has 50% sensitivity, 90.7% specificity
      Test protocol: 1:10 or 1:100 dilution contrast media
      Citation: Schrijvers et al101
    Row 7:
      Test: Drug Challenge—Immediate and non-immediate HR
      Test outcomes: 93.1% of patients tolerate challenge to skin test negative contrast media
      Test protocol: Various challenge protocols; e.g., two-step challenge with 5 and 30mL dose separated by 15min
      Citation: Ahn et al105
  Summary: Overview of available allergy tests for contrast media hypersensitivity, including their sensitivity, specificity, and protocols.
  Clinical relevance: Skin prick and intradermal testing have limited sensitivity; drug provocation testing remains the gold standard but is logistically challenging. These tests may be considered in select cases but are not routinely recommended over contrast switching.
